1The Whole Project in One Page

Read this first. Every presenter should be able to tell this story in one minute, because the professor may ask any of you how your part fits in.

The Problem

Cars such as the Mahindra BE 6 and XEV 9e can already park themselves (Autopark: 12 ultrasonic sensors, perpendicular, angled and parallel bays). A truck with a trailer cannot, and it is the vehicle that needs help most. The reason is physics: a tractor-trailer is two bodies joined at a hitch, and when it reverses, the hitch angle grows on its own. A 2° error becomes 60° after 28 m of reversing. If nobody corrects it, the trailer folds against the cab: a jackknife.

What We Built

A guidance system that takes a tractor-trailer from the yard gate into a chosen bay while the hitch angle never exceeds 60°. It has four layers:

LayerWhat it doesPresented in
Vehicle modelFour numbers describe the rig; four equations say how they change for a given speed and steeringPart 1 (A), Part 2 (B)
Hybrid A* plannerSearches the yard once and returns a route the truck can actually drive, gate to bayPart 3 (C)
NMPC controllerEvery 0.25 s, predicts 9.6 s ahead and chooses the steering that follows the route with |ψ| ≤ 60° as a hard limitPart 3 (C)
Driver guidanceTurns the controller's output into gear, speed (km/h), steering-wheel turns and distancePart 4 (D)

The Result

We tested 110 free bays (4 layouts × 6 random fills of parked trucks). All 110 were parked within tolerance, the hitch limit was never broken (worst case 50.1°), and a driver model without hitch awareness jackknifed on all 72 reversing manoeuvres.

The Chain of Ideas

THE STORY IN FOUR SENTENCES

(1) We model the truck as a wheeled robot with four state variables and two inputs. (2) Its kinematics show that reversing is unstable: the hitch angle grows exponentially. (3) So we plan a drivable route with Hybrid A* and follow it with an NMPC that looks ahead and treats the hitch limit as a hard constraint. (4) The result parks every test bay and tells a human driver exactly what to do.

SymbolMeaningValue
x1​,y1​Position of the tractor's rear-axle centremetres
θ0​, θ1​Heading of the tractor, heading of the trailer (from the x axis, anticlockwise positive)radians or degrees
ψ=θ0​−θ1​Hitch angle: how far the tractor is turned relative to the trailerhard limit 60°
v, δSpeed (negative in reverse), front-wheel steering angle∣v∣≤2 m/s, ∣δ∣≤35°
L1​, L2​, dTractor wheelbase, hitch to trailer axle, hitch ahead of the rear axle4 m, 8 m, 0.5 m

2What Your Part Must Achieve

Person A gives the professor the symbols: state X=[x1​,y1​,θ0​,ψ]T, input U=[v,δ]T. You give him the four equations X˙=f(X,U), show where each comes from, and end with the single most important fact of the project:

YOUR HEADLINE

Linearising the hitch equation gives ψ˙​≈−L2​v​ψ. The eigenvalue λ=−v/L2​ is negative going forward (stable) and positive in reverse (unstable): a 2° error grows to 60° in 28 m. That is why Part 3 needs a planner and a predictive controller.

The four equations you will derive:

x˙1​y˙​1​θ˙0​ψ˙​​=vcosθ0​=vsinθ0​=L1​v​tanδ=v[L1​tanδ​−L2​sinψ​−L1​L2​dtanδcosψ​]​

3The Maths Toolkit

Everything in this guide uses only the tools below. Learn them first; the derivations are then just bookkeeping.

3.1 Heading and Sideways Unit Vectors

u^(θ)=(cosθsinθ​),n^(θ)=(−sinθcosθ​)

Both have length 1 and are perpendicular: u^⋅n^=0.

3.2 Differentiating a Rotating Unit Vector

If the heading changes with time, θ=θ(t), the chain rule gives

dtd​u^(θ)=(−sinθcosθ​)θ˙=θ˙n^(θ)

Meaning: when a body rotates at rate θ˙, a point a distance r along its axis moves sideways at speed rθ˙. This one rule produces every rotation term in this guide.

3.3 Dot Products Between Two Headings

The dot product picks out the component of one vector along another. Using cos(a−b)=cosacosb+sinasinb and sin(a−b)=sinacosb−cosasinb:

u^(a)⋅u^(b)u^(a)⋅n^(b)n^(a)⋅n^(b)​=cosacosb+sinasinb=cos(a−b)=−cosasinb+sinacosb=sin(a−b)=sinasinb+cosacosb=cos(a−b)​

With a=θ0​ and b=θ1​, the difference a−b is exactly the hitch angle ψ. That is why sinψ and cosψ appear in the trailer equation.

3.4 Small-Angle Approximations

For an angle x in radians close to 0: sinx≈x, cosx≈1, tanx≈x. (At 10° the error of sinx≈x is only 0.5 %.) Always use radians in formulas: 1°=π/180≈0.01745 rad.

3.5 The Exponential Solution

The equation ψ˙​=λψ has the solution ψ(t)=ψ0​eλt. If λ<0, ψ dies out; if λ>0, it grows, multiplying by e≈2.72 every 1/λ seconds and doubling every ln2/λ seconds.

4The Tractor: Kinematic Bicycle Model

4.1 The Bicycle Simplification

A real tractor has two front wheels and two (or four) rear wheels. If the steering is designed properly (Ackermann geometry), all wheels turn about one common point, and the left and right wheels of an axle behave like a single wheel at the axle's centre. So we draw the tractor as a bicycle: one rear wheel, one steered front wheel, L1​ apart.

4.2 Rear Axle: the First Two Equations

The rear wheel cannot slide sideways (Person A's no-slip constraint), so its velocity points exactly along the heading:

p˙​1​=vu^(θ0​)⟹x˙1​=vcosθ0​,y˙​1​=vsinθ0​

This is also the definition of v: the signed speed of the rear-axle centre, negative in reverse.

4.3 Front Axle: the Turning-Rate Equation, by Vectors

1

Front-axle position: pf​=p1​+L1​u^(θ0​).

2

Differentiate, using rule 3.2:

p˙​f​=vu^(θ0​)+L1​θ˙0​n^(θ0​)
3

The front wheel points at θ0​+δ and cannot slide sideways, so the velocity has no component along n^(θ0​+δ):

p˙​f​⋅n^(θ0​+δ)=0
4

Use the dot products of 3.3 with a=θ0​, b=θ0​+δ, so a−b=−δ:

u^(θ0​)⋅n^(θ0​+δ)=sin(−δ)=−sinδ,n^(θ0​)⋅n^(θ0​+δ)=cosδ
5

Substitute:

−vsinδ+L1​θ˙0​cosδ=0⟹θ˙0​=L1​v​tanδ​

4.4 The Same Result from the ICR Geometry

Every wheel rolls on a circle around the ICR, so each wheel's axle line passes through it. The rear axle line is perpendicular to the body; the front axle line is perpendicular to the front wheel. In Figure 2 this makes a right-angled triangle with the body L1​ as one side and the turning radius R (rear axle to ICR) as the other, and the angle at the ICR equals δ (two lines each turned by δ make the same angle). So

tanδ=RL1​​ ⟹ R=tanδL1​​,θ˙0​=Rv​=L1​v​tanδ

The second step is the rule for any circle: angular rate = speed ÷ radius. Both methods agree; use whichever you can draw faster on a board.

Numbers: at full lock, δ=35°: R=4/tan35°=4/0.700=5.71 m, the tightest circle the rear axle can drive. At δ=0: R→∞, straight line, θ˙0​=0.

5The Trailer: Hitch and No-Slip

1

Hitch position and velocity. The hitch is d ahead of the rear axle on the tractor:

ph​=p1​+du^(θ0​)⟹p˙​h​=vu^(θ0​)+dθ˙0​n^(θ0​)
2

Trailer-axle position and velocity. The trailer axle is L2​ behind the hitch along the trailer:

p2​=ph​−L2​u^(θ1​)⟹p˙​2​=p˙​h​−L2​θ˙1​n^(θ1​)
3

No-slip at the trailer axle: no velocity along the trailer's sideways direction:

p˙​2​⋅n^(θ1​)=0 ⟹ p˙​h​⋅n^(θ1​)−L2​θ˙1​=1n^(θ1​)⋅n^(θ1​)​​=0 ⟹ θ˙1​=L2​p˙​h​⋅n^(θ1​)​

The numerator is exactly v⊥​ in Figure 4: the sideways part of the hitch velocity.

4

Compute v⊥​ with 3.3, a=θ0​, b=θ1​, a−b=ψ:

v⊥​=vsinψu^(θ0​)⋅n^(θ1​)​​+dθ˙0​cosψn^(θ0​)⋅n^(θ1​)​​=vsinψ+dθ˙0​cosψ
5

Result:

θ˙1​=L2​vsinψ+dθ˙0​cosψ​​
SAY IT LIKE THIS

"The trailer is dragged by its hitch. Split the hitch velocity into a part along the trailer and a part across it. The trailer axle can only roll, so the along part just pulls the trailer straight, and the across part swings it about its axle, with lever arm L2​. That gives θ˙1​=v⊥​/L2​."

Extra, if asked: the trailer axle's own speed is the along part, v2​=p˙​h​⋅u^(θ1​)=vcosψ−dθ˙0​sinψ. For a straight rig (ψ=0) it equals v, as expected.

6The Hitch-Angle Equation

6.1 Assemble It

Since ψ=θ0​−θ1​, its rate is ψ˙​=θ˙0​−θ˙1​. Substitute θ˙0​=L1​v​tanδ into both places:

ψ˙​=L1​v​tanδ−L2​vsinψ​−L2​dcosψ​⋅L1​v​tanδ=v[L1​tanδ​−L2​sinψ​−L1​L2​dtanδcosψ​]

A useful factored form (group the two steering terms):

ψ˙​=v[L1​tanδ​(1−L2​d​cosψ)−L2​sinψ​]

6.2 What Each Term Means

TermPhysical meaningSize in our rig
L1​tanδ​ (steering)The tractor's own turning. It is the only term the driver controls.Up to tan35°/4=0.175 per m
−L2​sinψ​ (hitch)The trailer's reaction: it swings to line up behind the hitch. Restoring forward, destabilising in reverse (Section 8).Up to 1/8=0.125 per m
−L1​L2​dtanδcosψ​ (offset)Appears only because the hitch is ahead of the rear axle; when the tractor turns, the hitch moves sideways and nudges the trailer.d/L2​=6% of the steering term

6.3 Sanity Checks (Do These Out Loud If Asked)

CheckWhat the formula givesMakes sense?
Unitsv [m/s] × [1/m] = [1/s]: a rate of angle in rad/sYes
Parked, v=0ψ˙​=0: nothing movesYes
Straight rig, straight wheels (ψ=0, δ=0)ψ˙​=0: it stays straightYes
Hitch over the axle, d=0ψ˙​=v[L1​tanδ​−L2​sinψ​]: the textbook formYes
Very long trailer, L2​→∞ψ˙​→θ˙0​: the trailer barely turnsYes
Reverse gear, v→−vEvery term flips signSee Section 8

7The Complete Model, and How We Simulate It

7.1 Every Term Is Proportional to v

Look at the four equations: each right-hand side has a factor v. Divide by v and write ds=vdt for the (signed) distance travelled:

dsdx1​​=cosθ0​,dsdy1​​=sinθ0​,dsdθ0​​=L1​tanδ​,dsdψ​=L1​tanδ​(1−L2​d​cosψ)−L2​sinψ​

Consequence: the shape of the path depends only on the steering along the distance, not on how fast you drive. Driving the same steering twice as fast traces the same path in half the time. That is why the planner chooses the path first and a speed profile separately.

7.2 Integrating with RK4

The equations give rates; to predict the future we integrate them in small time steps Δt. We use the classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta method (RK4), holding v and δ constant over each step:

k1​k3​Xk+1​​=f(Xk​),=f(Xk​+2Δt​k2​),=Xk​+6Δt​(k1​+2k2​+2k3​+k4​)​k2​k4​​=f(Xk​+2Δt​k1​),=f(Xk​+Δtk3​),​

It samples the slope four times per step and averages them, so its error per step shrinks like Δt5 (Euler's method, which uses only k1​, shrinks like Δt2). We use 0.05 s steps in the simulator, 0.4 s steps inside the NMPC prediction and 0.5 m steps in the planner's motion primitives. One model, one integrator, shared by planner, controller and viewer.

8Why Reversing Is Unstable

8.1 Linearise Around the Straight Rig

Hold the steering straight, δ=0. The hitch equation becomes

ψ˙​=−L2​v​sinψ

Its equilibrium is ψ=0. Near it, sinψ≈ψ:

ψ˙​≈λψ,λ=−L2​v​,ψ(t)=ψ0​eλt
GearEigenvalueBehaviour (at 1 m/s, L2​ = 8 m)
Forward, v>0λ=−v/L2​<0Stable. Any hitch angle decays with time constant L2​/v = 8 s. A towed trailer straightens itself.
Reverse, v<0λ=∣v∣/L2​>0Unstable. The angle grows ×e every 8 m, doubles every L2​ln2=5.5 m.

With steering included, the linearisation is ψ˙​≈−L2​v​ψ+L1​v​(1−L2​d​)δ: the first term is the instability, the second is how steering pushes on it.

SAY IT LIKE THIS

"The hitch term is minus v over L2​ times ψ. Going forward it pulls ψ back to zero, like a trailer following the truck. In reverse v is negative, the sign flips, and the term pushes ψ away from zero, like balancing a broom on your hand. The eigenvalue is positive, so any small error grows exponentially."

8.2 The Exact Solution (Not Only Near Zero)

We do not need the approximation. Write the equation in distance: reversing, ds=∣v∣dt and v=−∣v∣, so

dsdψ​=L2​sinψ​⟹∫sinψdψ​=∫L2​ds​

The standard integral is ∫sinψdψ​=ln​tan2ψ​​. You can check it by differentiating, using sinψ=2sin2ψ​cos2ψ​:

dψd​lntan2ψ​=tan2ψ​1​⋅2cos22ψ​1​=2sin2ψ​cos2ψ​1​=sinψ1​

So

lntan2ψ​−lntan2ψ0​​=L2​s​⟹tan2ψ​=tan2ψ0​​es/L2​​(reverse)

Forward, the exponent is −s/L2​ and the angle decays. For small angles, tan(ψ/2)≈ψ/2 and this becomes ψ≈ψ0​es/L2​, the linear result again.

8.3 The Numbers on the Slide

Solve for the distance: s=L2​lntan(ψ0​/2)tan(ψ/2)​. Starting from a 2° error (ψ0​/2=1°):

ReachCalculationDistance reversed
60° (our hard limit)8lntan1°tan30°​=8ln0.017460.5774​=8ln33.08=8×3.49928.0 m
75° (physical jackknife)8lntan1°tan37.5°​=8ln43.96=8×3.78330.3 m

Why this matters: a bay approach is 20 to 40 m of reversing. Without correction, any small error becomes a jackknife within one manoeuvre. A controller must act early, before the error grows, which means it must look ahead: that is the motivation for NMPC in Part 3.

9How Much Steering Holds a Hitch Angle

To hold the hitch at a constant angle (for example while reversing round a curve), set ψ˙​=0 in the factored equation (with v=0):

L1​tanδ​(1−L2​d​cosψ)=L2​sinψ​⟹tanδhold​=L2​L1​​⋅1−L2​d​cosψsinψ​

At ψ = 60°: tanδ=0.5×1−0.0625×0.50.866​=0.9690.433​=0.447, so δhold​=24.1°.

The largest angle steering can hold. Let c=d/L2​=0.0625 and g(ψ)=1−ccosψsinψ​. Differentiate (quotient rule):

g′(ψ)=(1−ccosψ)2cosψ(1−ccosψ)−sinψ(csinψ)​=(1−ccosψ)2cosψ−c​

(using cos2+sin2=1). It is zero at cosψ∗=c, so ψ∗=86.4°, where g=1/1−c2​=1.002. Then tanδmax​=0.5×1.002, so δ=26.6°.

WHY THE LIMIT IS 60°

To straighten a hitch you must steer more than the holding angle. At 60° holding needs 24.1°, leaving about 11° of lock to pull the trailer back. Much beyond 60° there is too little margin, and past about 86° no steering can even hold the angle. So the controller treats 60° as a hard limit and the planner stays below 52°.

10Why Reversing Feels Backwards

Drivers learn "to reverse the trailer left, first steer right". The equations show why. Reverse (v=−1 m/s) with constant left steering δ=+10° from a straight rig:

  • θ˙0​=vtanδ/L1​<0: the tractor heading turns clockwise straight away.
  • That makes ψ negative, and then θ˙1​≈vsinψ/L2​>0: the trailer heading turns the other way.

In control language, the tractor's rear axle is a non-minimum-phase output in reverse: to move the trailer one way, the tractor must first move the other way. A controller that only reacts to the current error (like PID) steers the wrong way at first. This is why our NMPC tracks the trailer axle (Person C will mention it).

QuantityCalculationResult
x˙1​−1×cos10°=−0.985−0.985 m/s
y˙​1​−1×sin10°=−0.174−0.174 m/s
θ˙0​−1×0.2679/4−0.0670 rad/s (−3.84°/s)
Steering term0.2679/40.06699
Hitch term0.3420/80.04275

12The Derivation on a Board, in Six Lines

  1. u^=(cosθ,sinθ), n^=(−sinθ,cosθ), dtd​u^=θ˙n^.
  2. Rear axle rolls: p˙​1​=vu^0​ ⇒ x˙1​=vcosθ0​, y˙​1​=vsinθ0​.
  3. Front wheel rolls: (vu^0​+L1​θ˙0​n^0​)⋅n^(θ0​+δ)=0 ⇒ −vsinδ+L1​θ˙0​cosδ=0 ⇒ θ˙0​=vtanδ/L1​.
  4. Hitch: p˙​h​=vu^0​+dθ˙0​n^0​. Trailer axle rolls: p˙​2​⋅n^1​=0 ⇒ θ˙1​=p˙​h​⋅n^1​/L2​.
  5. u^0​⋅n^1​=sinψ, n^0​⋅n^1​=cosψ ⇒ θ˙1​=(vsinψ+dθ˙0​cosψ)/L2​.
  6. ψ˙​=θ˙0​−θ˙1​=v[L1​tanδ​−L2​sinψ​−L1​L2​dtanδcosψ​]; at δ=0, small ψ: ψ˙​≈−L2​v​ψ.

Slide 12 · The Complete Four-State Model (about 1 min)

14Questions the Professor May Ask

Derive ψ˙​ on the board.
Use the six lines in Section 12. Start from the no-slip constraints, not from the final formula.
Why does tanδ appear and not δ?
From the ICR triangle: tanδ=L1​/R. For small angles tanδ≈δ, but at 35° the difference is 14 %.
What is the eigenvalue and what does it mean?
λ=−v/L2​ from linearising at ψ=0, δ=0. Its sign decides stability: negative forward, positive in reverse. 1/∣λ∣ is the time for a ×e change: 8 s at 1 m/s.
Is the system stable forward?
The hitch angle is: a trailer straightens behind a truck driving forward. Position and heading are not "stable" in any sense; they just follow the steering.
Why does speed not appear in the 28 m figure?
Every term is proportional to v, so in terms of distance the growth is the same at any speed: ×e every L2​ metres. Faster reversing only makes it happen sooner in time.
What does the offset d do?
With the hitch ahead of the rear axle, steering moves the hitch sideways, which slightly rotates the trailer the same way. It reduces the steering term by (1−L2​d​cosψ), about 6 %.
Why 60° as the limit?
Holding 60° needs 24.1° of steering, leaving ~11° of our 35° lock to recover; beyond about 86° no steering can hold the angle. The physical jackknife is 75°.
What is non-minimum phase here?
In reverse, the tractor initially moves opposite to where the trailer must go (Figure 7). Reactive control steers the wrong way first; we track the trailer axle instead.
Why RK4 and not Euler?
Fourth-order accuracy at the 0.4 s prediction steps the NMPC uses; Euler would need much smaller steps for the same accuracy. RK4 costs four evaluations of a cheap function.
What if the wheels slip?
Then the no-slip constraints, and the model, break. At ≤ 2 m/s on dry asphalt slip is centimetres, inside our 0.25 m clearance. Ice or speed would need a dynamic tyre model.

15Check Yourself

  1. Compute the turning radius of the rear axle at δ=20°.
  2. Show that n^(a)⋅u^(b)=−sin(a−b).
  3. With δ=0 and ψ=10°, reversing at 1 m/s, what is ψ˙​ in °/s? Is the angle growing or shrinking?
  4. How many metres of reversing does it take for a 1° hitch error to reach 60° (straight wheels)?
  5. What steering holds ψ=30°?
  6. If L2​ were 12 m instead of 8 m, would reversing be more or less forgiving? By how much?

Answers

  1. R=4/tan20°=4/0.364=11.0 m.
  2. n^(a)⋅u^(b)=−sinacosb+cosasinb=−(sinacosb−cosasinb)=−sin(a−b).
  3. ψ˙​=−L2​v​sinψ=−8−1​×0.1736=+0.0217 rad/s =+1.24°/s. Positive and ψ is positive, so it is growing.
  4. s=8lntan0.5°tan30°​=8ln0.0087270.5774​=8ln66.2=33.5 m.
  5. tanδ=0.5×1−0.0625×0.8660.5​=0.9460.25​=0.264, so δ=14.8°.
  6. More forgiving: the error grows ×e every L2​ metres, so every 12 m instead of 8 m (50 % more distance). Longer trailers are easier to reverse, which drivers also say.

16One-Page Cheat Sheet

The Model

x˙1​=vcosθ0​,y˙​1​=vsinθ0​,θ˙0​=L1​v​tanδ,ψ˙​=v[L1​tanδ​−L2​sinψ​−L1​L2​dtanδcosψ​]

Where Each Comes From

Rear axle rolls along its heading. Front wheel rolls along θ0​+δ ⇒ R=L1​/tanδ, θ˙0​=v/R. Trailer axle rolls ⇒ θ˙1​=v⊥​/L2​, v⊥​=vsinψ+dθ˙0​cosψ. Then ψ˙​=θ˙0​−θ˙1​.

Tools

dtd​u^=θ˙n^; u^(a)⋅n^(b)=sin(a−b); n^(a)⋅n^(b)=cos(a−b).

Instability

δ=0, small ψ: ψ˙​≈−L2​v​ψ, λ=−v/L2​. Forward stable, reverse unstable: ×e every 8 m, doubles every 5.5 m. Exact: tan2ψ​=tan2ψ0​​es/L2​; 2° → 60° in 28.0 m, → 75° in 30.3 m.

Holding and the Limit

tanδhold​=L2​L1​​1−L2​d​cosψsinψ​: 24.1° at 60°, maximum 26.6° (at 86°). Limit 60° leaves ~11° of 35° lock to recover.

Numbers

L1​ = 4 m, L2​ = 8 m, d = 0.5 m, Rmin​ = 5.71 m at 35°. RK4: 0.05 s (simulation), 0.4 s (NMPC), 0.5 m (planner).
